style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive prose) + selective amplified study form; narrative register; no divine name inserted
chapterNote: The day set for the Jews' slaughter arrives — and is overturned. On the very date Haman chose by lot for their destruction, the Jews stand and are delivered instead; three times the narrator notes they took no plunder, marking this as defense, not greed. Out of the reversal comes Purim, named from the 'lot' Haman cast: a yearly feast of gladness, gifts to one another, and charity to the poor, so that a people rescued by an unnamed but unmistakable Hand would never forget the month turned from mourning to joy.

1.text: On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, when the king's command and decree were to be carried out — the very day the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them — the reverse took place: the Jews overpowered those who hated them.
1.amp: on the day the enemies of the Jews hoped to master them, it was turned about [nehpokh hu — it was overturned], so that the Jews themselves mastered those who hated them.
1.notes: 'It was overturned' (nehpokh hu) is the book's great theme-word. The date engineered for genocide becomes the date of rescue; the whole story is this single reversal writ large. The lot that fell to a day of death has, unseen, been overruled to a day of life.

2.text: Throughout every province of King Ahasuerus the Jews assembled in their cities to strike at those who had sought to do them harm. No one could withstand them, for dread of them had come over all the peoples.

3.text: And all the officials of the provinces — the satraps, the governors, and those who did the king's work — supported the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them.

4.text: For Mordecai was powerful in the palace, and his fame spread through all the provinces, as the man Mordecai grew greater and greater.

5.text: So the Jews struck down all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying, and dealt with those who hated them as they pleased.

6.text: Within the citadel of Susa the Jews put to death and wiped out five hundred men,

9.text: Parmashta and Arisai, Aridai and Vaizatha —

10.text: the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the persecutor of the Jews. Yet on the plunder they laid no hand.
10.notes: The house of the Agagite falls completely — all ten sons named and gone, the line that carried the old Amalekite enmity ended. And pointedly, 'they laid no hand on the plunder,' though the decree allowed it (8:11): unlike Saul, who spared Agag and seized Amalek's spoil (1 Sam. 15), these Jews take nothing. This is defense and justice, not greed.

11.text: That same day the number of those killed in the fortress of Susa was reported to the king.

12.text: And the king said to Queen Esther, "In the fortress of Susa alone the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men, along with the ten sons of Haman. What must they have done in the rest of the king's provinces? Now what is your petition? It will be granted. What further request do you have? It will be done."

13.text: "If it please the king," Esther answered, "let the Jews in Susa be allowed to act tomorrow as well, according to today's decree; and let Haman's ten sons be hanged on the gallows."

14.text: The king ordered this to be done. The decree was issued in Susa, and they hanged the ten sons of Haman.

15.text: The Jews in Susa gathered again on the fourteenth day of Adar and killed three hundred men in Susa, but they laid no hand on the plunder.

16.text: Meanwhile the rest of the Jews throughout the king's provinces also gathered to defend their lives and win relief from their enemies. They killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but they laid no hand on the plunder.
16.notes: A third time — 'they laid no hand on the plunder.' The refrain will not let the reader mistake this for a massacre of appetite. The vast number reflects how many still chose to attack a people already known to be under a mysterious protection; those who came to kill fell instead.

17.text: All this took place on the thirteenth of Adar; then on the fourteenth they rested, making it a day of feasting and rejoicing.

18.text: But the Jews in Susa had gathered on the thirteenth and the fourteenth, and rested on the fifteenth, making that a day of feasting and gladness.

19.text: This is why the Jews of the villages, who live in the unwalled towns, keep the fourteenth day of Adar as a day of gladness and feasting, a holiday for sending portions of food to one another.

20.text: Mordecai recorded these things and sent letters to all the Jews in every province of King Ahasuerus, near and far,

21.text: binding them to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar every year,

22.text: as the days on which the Jews gained relief from their enemies, and the month that was turned for them from sorrow to gladness and from mourning to a holiday — that they should make them days of feasting and joy, of sending portions to one another and gifts to the poor.
22.amp: the month which was turned for them [nehpakh — overturned] from sorrow to gladness and from mourning to a good day [yom tov — a holiday].
22.notes: Purim's shape is set here: not merely relief, but gladness that overflows outward — 'portions to one another and gifts to the poor.' A deliverance received is a deliverance shared; the joy of the rescued spends itself on neighbor and pauper alike.

23.text: So the Jews took up as a custom what they had begun to do, and what Mordecai had written to them.

24.text: For Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the foe of all the Jews, had schemed to destroy them and had cast the Pur — that is, the lot — to rout and ruin them.
24.notes: The summary names the buried theology of the whole book: Haman cast the Pur, the lot, trusting blind chance to pick the killing-day. But 'the lot is cast into the lap, and its every decision is from the LORD' (Prov. 16:33). What Haman gave to chance, the unnamed God quietly governed to deliverance.

25.text: But when it came before the king, he ordered by letter that the wicked scheme Haman had devised against the Jews should recoil on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.

26.text: This is why these days are called Purim, from the word Pur. Because of all that was written in this letter, and all they had seen and experienced in the matter,
26.notes: The festival is named, of all things, for Haman's lot — 'Purim.' Israel's feast of deliverance carries in its very name the memory that their enemy's dice were overruled. Every year the name itself confesses a providence the book never spells out.

27.text: the Jews bound themselves, their descendants, and all who joined them to a custom that could not lapse: to keep these two days every year, as written and at their appointed time.

28.text: These days were to be remembered and kept in every generation, by every family, in every province and every city — so that these days of Purim would never fall into disuse among the Jews, nor their memory die out among their descendants.

29.text: Then Queen Esther, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote a second time, with all their authority, to give this letter about Purim its full force.

30.text: And letters were sent to all the Jews in the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, with words of peace and truth,

31.text: to establish these days of Purim at their appointed times, just as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had enjoined on them, and just as they had laid down for themselves and their descendants, with their appointed fasts and their lamenting.

32.text: So Esther's decree confirmed these regulations for Purim, and it was written in the record.
